artifacts.synopsis: Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the divestiture because BCO 38-3(a) had already ended Presbytery's jurisdiction while he was in good standing and under no investigation or charges. It directed Presbytery to record the irregular withdrawal, acknowledge his new membership, and remove him from its roll.

artifacts.title: Myers v. Illiana Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: An elder appealed Presbytery’s elevation, without additional process, of suspensions from office and the Sacraments to deposition and excommunication. The SJC granted the appeal, reversed in whole, and remanded, restoring the prior suspensions. Elevation required a hearing on incorrigibility and contumacy—with a charge, evidence, plea, and defense—but not a full de novo trial; disagreement with the original verdict alone was insufficient. The SJC left unresolved deposition from office when excommunication is absent.

artifacts.title: Benyola v. Central Florida Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC declared Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order, because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The decision was adopted 23-0 on a roll call, one absent, on the officers' recommendation. The record does not identify the underlying presbytery action or reach the complaint's merits, so the case's value is its threshold standing ruling, not any complaint determination.

artifacts.title: Harrell et al. v. Covenant Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

artifacts.synopsis: Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s action because discipline preceded particular charges and a specific confession, and because an independent church lacked authority to impose PCA censure. It declared the underlying matter moot because the alleged event was twenty-one years old and the victim would not cooperate, ending the proceeding without remand. The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically.

It found him not guilty on every charge because the prosecution failed to meet its burden, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to good standing. For the lawsuit charge, it rejected a categorical ban on civil suits between Christians and required proof that this suit was sinful.

artifacts.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

artifacts.synopsis: Ryan Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its refusal to commence process against Greg Johnson on four allegations concerning same-sex attraction as sin, identity in Christ, sanctification, and fitness for office. The SJC denied the complaint in full. It found no clear procedural error and held that Johnson’s explanations and clarifications made Presbytery’s non-indictment judgments reasonable. No trial was ordered. The ruling neither adjudged Johnson guilty nor endorsed every statement or broader constitutional position concerning same-sex attraction.

The SJC denied all five specifications of error and upheld the Presbytery's decision in whole.

artifacts.title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

artifacts.title: Evans and Pitts et al. v. Arizona Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Arizona Presbytery deposed TE Evans under BCO 38-1 without properly securing his approval of the full statement of facts, as the Investigative Committee's report added additional adverse facts he had not seen or approved. The SJC sustained the complaints of Evans and Pitts et al., annulled the deposition, and remanded the matter to AZP for action consistent with BCO 38-1 requirements; a lengthy concurring opinion by RE Donahoe extensively analyzed BCO 38-1 confession procedures.

artifacts.synopsis: A minister appealed a judgment finding him guilty on most charges and imposing six months’ suspension. The SJC held BCO 32-20 barred Specifications 1, 2, and 4 because Presbytery lacked extraordinary justification for prosecuting old allegations, but did not bar ongoing Specification 3. It separately found the entire process constitutionally flawed and prejudicial. The SJC reversed the whole censure, declined Presbytery’s requested harsher sentence, and concluded the matter. A concurrence disputed the majority’s BCO 32-20 interpretation while agreeing with the result.

artifacts.synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 matter, the SJC held that a presbytery erred in upholding a session's erasure of a member who pled not guilty to failing to submit and pursued divorce. The session wrongly equated declining divorce counsel with refusing submission, failed to assess membership duties in another branch, failed to notify her of erasure, and proceeded without process after dropping charges. The SJC sustained the challenge, directed the session to note the notice failure and remove her under BCO 38-3(a), but ordered no express reversal.

artifacts.synopsis: An indicted teaching elder challenged Chesapeake Presbytery’s approval of a PJC judgment and indefinite suspension after the PJC blended a BCO 32 case of process with a BCO 38-1 case without process. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled Presbytery’s approval, and returned the matter to the PJC. Because he admitted only some indicted charges, his negotiated confession could not satisfy BCO 38-1 and the conversion prejudiced his rights. The PJC may dismiss or proceed under BCO 32; the ruling does not decide whether conversion is ever permissible.

artifacts.title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

artifacts.synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

artifacts.synopsis: TE John Hardie appealed his Metro Atlanta Presbytery conviction on three charges of breaking ordination vows and indefinite suspension, alleging seventeen procedural and evidentiary errors. Applying BCO 39-2/3 clear-error deference, the SJC denied every specification and upheld the judgment and censure. It found no clear error in the BCO 31-2 investigation, indictment/prosecutor process, commission membership, evidence rulings, scheduling, alleged prejudice, or censure. It assessed transcription costs equally while encouraging MAP to absorb them, and cautioned that an absent commissioner's vote might support a future challenge.

artifacts.title: Presbyterian Church in America v. South Florida Presbytery (Citation)
artifacts.synopsis: Reviewing South Florida Presbytery’s response to a General Assembly citation, the SJC found most responses satisfactory but rejected one because it did not address BCO 32-2’s requirement to proceed once a charge is made. It approved previously unsubmitted 2009 executive-session minutes with an exception because their treatment of a teaching elder appeared to violate BCO 46-8. Presbytery also had to submit amended minutes and complete, or formally plan, overdue Session-record reviews for report to the 45th General Assembly.

The decisive reason was procedural: the record did not show timely service of the indictment/citations or the required 14-day trial notice, violating BCO 32-3, 32-7, and 32-10. Under BCO 42-9, the SJC rendered the decision it thought should have been made, finding no strong presumption of guilt under BCO 31-2 justified formal process; it added pastoral counsel, expressly not censure.

artifacts.synopsis: Korean Eastern Presbytery dismissed TE Eliot Lee's charges against two teaching elders without trial, and the SJC sustained Lee's complaint that this was unconstitutional. Although a presbytery may dismiss charges under BCO 29-1, 32-20, 34-2, or 31-8, it bears the burden of documenting that basis; KEP did not. The SJC refused Lee's request that it enter the guilt verdicts the presbytery should have reached—that power exists on appeal, not complaint. It remanded for KEP to begin process under BCO 32.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC dismissed Matt Ruff's complaint against Nashville Presbytery as judicially out of order under OMSJC 10.5.a. Ruff challenged Presbytery's failure to investigate a teaching elder, but BCO 43 requires a complaint against an act or decision; lack of action qualifies only when a court meeting has occurred and the court failed to act. Presbytery's nearest antecedent meeting was August 18, 2010, and Ruff filed October 27, 2010, beyond BCO 43-2's thirty-day limit. Because the defect could not be cured, the case was dismissed without reaching the merits; a separate objection disputed that ruling.

artifacts.synopsis: Northern California Presbytery adopted an abstract resolution declaring six different views on the diaconate permissible for ministers and Sessions; the SJC sustained the complaints and annulled the resolution, holding that no court may issue binding abstract decrees beyond its proper jurisdictional exercise. A concurring opinion analyzed each of the six diaconal views in detail and set out standards (the GUMP/Kniseley framework) for when diaconal assistant practices are constitutionally permissible.

artifacts.synopsis: Kirk Lyons filed BCO 32-2 charges against TE Craig Bulkeley with Western Carolina Presbytery. WCP dismissed the charges, then ruled Lyons's complaint administratively out of order for lack of standing. The SJC answered that the dismissal was not erroneous—Presbytery had discretion under BCO 31-8, 34-2, and 32-20, and the record showed no clear error—but that WCP erred on standing because Lyons's filing brought him under its jurisdiction. Because that error was not prejudicial, the SJC denied the complaint.

artifacts.title: McNeil v. Chesapeake Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied a censured husband's complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery's approval of a judicial commission report, which had upheld his session's refusal to receive his charges against his wife after she filed for civil divorce. Applying BCO 39-3.2–3.3, the SJC deferred to the lower courts' factual and discretionary findings absent clear error. It found no clear procedural error, upheld the conclusion that the wife did not sin by seeking civil protection, and invoked BCO 31-8's caution about accusations from one under censure.

artifacts.title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

artifacts.synopsis: A complaint challenged Siouxlands Presbytery's investigation of allegations that TE Joshua Moon held heterodox Federal Vision views and its finding of no strong presumption of guilt. The SJC held that Presbytery had investigated diligently under BCO 31-2 and, deferring under BCO 39-3 to its credibility judgment, found no clear error. It declined to decide whether the overture should have been treated as charges because that issue was not raised below, while leaving future charges possible. A concurrence favored charges; the dissent would have found error and remanded.

artifacts.title: Morton Smith v. Western Carolina
artifacts.synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

But Presbytery could not treat its authority to dissolve a pastoral relationship as authority to compel resignation on pain of discipline. The SJC therefore vacated the censure and dissolution of the call and remanded for reconsideration of censure; Grady's separate administrative suspension remained effective.

artifacts.synopsis: Chastain appealed Heritage Presbytery’s 2006 excommunication and deposition. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order because Chastain had renounced PCA jurisdiction on May 8, 2006. Consequently, Presbytery’s later proceedings were moot and SJC 2005-1 remained in effect. The SJC did not reach the merits. A concurrence questioned the discipline process after renunciation; a dissent argued the majority lacked constitutional authority to recognize unilateral withdrawal and thereby undercut discipline.

artifacts.title: Paul W. Lee v. Korean Southwest
artifacts.synopsis: A minister appealed three convictions and suspension that would automatically become indefinite absent repentance. The SJC sustained the appeal: unauthorized committee citations and admonition without process could not support guilt, and multiple trial violations were fatally prejudicial. It set aside the judgment, dismissed the citation and admonition charges, and revoked both censures. The inappropriate-language charge was not adjudicated on its merits; Presbytery could retry it on remand or dismiss it.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

artifacts.synopsis: In a dispute arising from a Korean Eastern Presbytery congregational election, two ruling elders were tried, refused to plead, and were suspended from sacraments and office; KEP denied their appeal, then increased the censures to deposition and excommunication for contumacy. The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The original suspension remained.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC decided whether a presbytery and its special judicial commission could assume original jurisdiction over disciplinary charges against a church member. It sustained the appeal and reversed: the court of original jurisdiction for communicant members is the local church session. The ruling rested on jurisdiction, not the merits; no remand was ordered.

It held that Presbytery could bring charges but could not substitute the Papua New Guinea criminal proceedings for ecclesiastical process, especially when it neither served an indictment and charges nor appointed counsel for an accused unable to attend. The remand permitted a constitutionally compliant trial; it did not resolve guilt or bar discipline.

The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed.
